toc.title: Every behavior is in service of survival
The vagus nerve is a conduit

sections.title: Two moments from my own life

toc.title: A new paradigm, and a new narrative

blocks.p: This is a return to the foundations of the Polyvagal Theory from Dr. Stephen Porges. Along the way you'll hear from two other people: Dr. Porges himself, who created the Polyvagal Theory, and Deb Dana, a therapist who's a very big name in the polyvagal space. I interviewed both of them on the podcast, and I've pulled a few of their words in where I think they add clarity, or just some weight, to what I'm saying.

We have to get this down before understanding anything else. The autonomic nervous system controls the body's internal environment: all the stuff you don't have to think about. Breathing, heart rate, hormone release, sweating, pupil dilation, digestion, salivation, and a whole bunch more.

No one is thinking about their pupils. Do you have any idea how much your pupils are or are not dilated right now? Do you have any idea what's going on with your digestion? Maybe you can feel it, but you don't guide it. Breathing you kind of can, but moment to moment, no one is typically planning their breathing.
So the autonomic nervous system controls the body's internal environment without conscious thought. But what's really important is that it can actually be used for different purposes.
The autonomic nervous system governs three basic states through biological pathways:

ol: The ventral vagal safe and social state. This governs social engagement. It's one of the parasympathetic branches.
The sympathetic flight and fight pathways. These are responsible for mobilization.
The dorsal vagal shutdown. This is the second parasympathetic system, and it governs the immobilization response.

blocks.p: These different biological pathways are responsible for responding to various levels of safety or danger. If we're safe, great, we use those pathways. If not, we use our mobilization pathways. And if that's not going to be successful, we use our immobilization pathways.
None of this is a choice. I really want to stress that. It's outside of our conscious control. We don't shift from social engagement to flight and fight because we choose to.

You can probably experience that right now. Close your eyes and think about a spider hanging behind you by its web. You might feel a shift within you. You might feel a little more tense. Your breathing might pause for a moment, if you're like me at least. If you did hold your breath or feel a little fear, those are autonomic shifts happening within you that you did not control. You simply responded to the image of a spider hanging behind you. And if that doesn't work for you, imagine whatever scares you behind you. You'll have some sort of reaction.

blocks.h: Every behavior is in service of survival

blocks.p: Deb Dana put it this way:

q: Every behavior is in service of survival... No matter how crazy it looks, your nervous system has enacted something because it's trying to keep you alive.
blocks.cite: Deb Dana, [Deb Dana Interview: Story Follows State, Climbing the Ladder and Diagnosing (episode 29)](https://player.captivate.fm/episode/f8b9643c-28f8-4185-9525-8b4e6301516c)

blocks.p: So let's start there. All of these autonomic responses are about survival. This is supposed to happen. We're supposed to shift from our safety pathways to our mobilization system, and if that doesn't work, into the immobilization system, the shutdown state, because it increases the chances of survival. All of these states do.

The autonomic nervous system shifts the biological pathways that are responsible for our behavioral states. It shifts automatically, outside of our conscious control, to increase our chances of survival.

This is pretty darn important, because it makes daily living and surviving possible for all mammals. This is a mammalian thing, not just a human thing. It's what lets mammals socially engage, live in families or herds, and build tribes.

Think about it: if it weren't autonomic, we'd have to consciously plan breathing and heart rate and hormone release, all in real time, all at the same time. We'd have to decide how much to tense our muscles when we're in danger, how much to sweat or whether to sweat at all, how fast to raise our heartbeat, how to adjust our breathing. And not just in that moment, but moment to moment, knowing when to calm things down and when to speed things up. I don't know how long we'd last. The autonomic nervous system is really good at this. It does it for us, and that frees our thinking minds for other things. That's not always helpful, but at least we have the opportunity to use our thinking potential to make life better for humans and other species.

These are the primary autonomic states: safe and social, flight and fight, and shutdown. Just like we have primary colors, red, yellow and blue, that you can mix to make other colors, we also have other states and mixed states. For now, we're working with the primary ones.
Your primary state is a reaction to a few different things.

The outside environment. That could be a dangerous environment or a dangerous person, a loud sound, dark lighting, or it could be happy people and a safe environment. Your state reacts to the sensory experience of the environment you're literally in: the way it sounds, the way it looks, the way it smells. All of those inputs can trigger your autonomic nervous system to shift into social behavior, flight and fight behavior, or shutdown behavior.

The internal environment. We can shift state based on what's happening within us. Chronic illness, for example, might put someone in more of a defensive state and take away their potential to be in their safe and social state, to socially engage, to feel happy and positive. When we're in pain, our capacity to socially engage is probably a lot less. If you bang your knee on something, you're not going to smile about it and laugh and connect with the person next to you. You'll be in pain, and probably have some defensive energy. Or if you don't eat and you get hungry enough, you become hangry. That fight system comes on to make you get food.

The interpersonal environment. This counts as environmental, but I think it's worth separating out. Between two or more people, there are cues of danger and cues of safety in big ways and small ways. It could be something as big as outward aggression or as simple as looking at a cell phone. If someone looks at their phone while you're talking to them, your capacity to feel socially engaged is diminished, at least in that moment. It can be fixed. It's not a huge deal. But it takes you out of your social engagement pathways for that moment.

Your perceptions of all of these. Our perceptions might not be an accurate reflection of the real world. They're our subjective filter. A football fan's reaction to a game is a lot different from someone who isn't a fan. Whatever happens on the screen might take the fan out of their social engagement system and into defensive flight and fight energy, or even into shutdown if it's a disaster, like the 49ers losing their past two Super Bowl appearances. For someone who isn't into football, one group of men scoring more points than another means nothing. Or take a Star Wars fan versus a non-Star Wars fan watching those terrible sequel trilogy movies. For those of us who are way into Star Wars, they're genuinely upsetting due to their awfulness. We're basically personally offended. Someone who isn't into Star Wars couldn't care less and just wants to enjoy the movie.

Here's a more serious example. Back then I worked at a public school, and one of my student clients lived in a neighborhood that was definitely more on the dangerous side. He was outside playing catch with his friends, throwing a football back and forth, and he heard a gunshot. His perception of a gunshot was way different from mine. In my neighborhood, that's not something we hear. If I heard a gunshot in his neighborhood, I'd get in my car and leave, or go into a house or somewhere safe. For him, it was, "Well, that's not about me. That's about somebody else." It didn't trigger his defensive energy the way it would for somebody else. His perception was different.
These states aren't just something we're in for a moment and then out of. We can stay in them for quite a long time, and while we're in them, we experience the world in significantly different ways.

In the safe and social state, we experience the world in a much more positive, hopeful, empathetic way. In a shutdown state, we're probably going to experience the world as a lot more hopeless. We're going to view ourselves as worthless. We're not going to feel much hope, or much of anything. It's a very disconnected state. We bring those filters to all of our interactions: with people, with companies, with family members, at school and at work. We bring them everywhere we go.

It's also possible to become stuck in the defensive states: sympathetic flight and fight, or parasympathetic shutdown. When we talk about trauma, that's really what we're talking about. Trauma is not the event, or the lack of events, that left us stuck. It's the stuck defensive state. It's the inability to get back up into the safe and social state. It's the impact of the event, not the event itself.

There's a metaphor for all of this called the [polyvagal ladder](piece:autonomic-nervous-system). It's from Deb Dana, the therapist who applied the Polyvagal Theory to therapy. It shows how the autonomic nervous system is stacked in the body, the hierarchy of these states.
Picture a ladder:

ul: At the top are the ventral vagal pathways, which control the safe and social state and its behaviors. That mirrors the body, because those pathways live in the head and neck and are connected to the heart.
In the middle are the flight and fight sympathetic pathways. Those live in the chest, and they govern the use of the arms and legs.
At the bottom are the dorsal vagal shutdown pathways. Those live in the gut. When something's not quite right, you'll feel that shutdown system come on in your gut.

blocks.p: It's also a great metaphor because we go up and down the ladder in sequential order. We don't skip. Again, this is not a choice. We're not choosing from a menu of options. We're going through a sequence of events.

Going down: if we can't stay in our safe and social state at the top of the ladder, we drop into our flight and fight system, and in that order, flight first. If we can't run away from whatever it is, then we fight. If we can't fight, we drop further, to the bottom of the ladder, into our shutdown state. This is where we immobilize, where we collapse. And all of these are about increasing the likelihood of surviving whatever's happening.

Going up, we have to go through each rung of the ladder too. We come up out of shutdown into flight and fight energy, but it's fight first. We have a sympathetic fight surge, then up into flight, which is also sympathetic, and then up into our safety state.

Does this look the same for everyone? Does it feel the same, with the same intensity? No. That's all very subjective, case by case. But that's the basic biological hierarchy and sequence that mammals go through.

blocks.h: The vagus nerve is a conduit

blocks.p: If you've spent any time learning about the Polyvagal Theory outside of this, you may have heard people talking about hacking the vagus nerve or stimulating the vagus nerve. I don't think that's the issue here. That's not the goal when it comes to best using the knowledge of the Polyvagal Theory, whether that's trauma healing, self-regulation, or anchoring yourself in the present moment.

Dr. Porges calls the vagus nerve a conduit. It's not the thing we're addressing in and of itself. As I listen to Dr. Porges, what I get out of it is that the brainstem is really the key to all of this. Take away the intelligence we give the nerve, and think in terms of a feedback loop: brainstem, through the vagus nerve, to the bodily organs and muscles, and then what those organs and muscles send back up through the vagus nerve to the brainstem. It's a communication loop. And the majority of that communication is actually from the body up to the brain, not the brain to the body. We put a lot of emphasis on brain stuff, but I think it's something like 80% of the fibers in the vagus nerve that carry communication from the body to the brain.
Here's how Dr. Porges put it:

q: The vagus nerve is a conduit. It's a wire. That's not what we're really concerned about. We're concerned about the regulator that's sending signals through that wire and the impact of those signals to the target organs, and then the target organs, through the sensory part of the vagus, sending signals back to the brain. So we're more concerned with the feedback loop between organ and brainstem that's going through the vagus than the nerve itself. So we get caught up, and the term I use is that we start giving executive function, decision-making properties, to the nerve. And we're literally obfuscating, blinding, covering up the real process, which is really a regulatory system that is a feedback between brainstem structures and... bodily organs.

Dr. Stephen Porges, [Dr Stephen Porges Interview: Mental Disorders, Substance Use, Psychiatry & the Polyvagal Theory (episode 15)](https://player.captivate.fm/episode/a3c6a54a-11a7-4f2f-9d74-db287c774d08)

blocks.p: The communication of safety or danger, brain to body and body to brain, is what's important. The vagus nerve is just the pathway the information is sent through. This is not about hacking or stimulating the vagus nerve.

The brainstem is the key point. We detect what's in the environment through our senses, and that goes to the brainstem. I don't like the word "decides," but the brainstem decides, based on that information, what level of safety or danger we're in. If it decides we're in danger, it reduces our potential for things like critical thinking and empathy. It also reduces our potential for getting close to other people, or breathing in a relaxed way. So it affects the brain and it affects the body. The brainstem is where the regulation of our bodily state occurs, and the effect of our bodily state goes back up to the brainstem. All the other brain structures sit on top of it, and as Dr. Porges says, what higher brain structures can do is in part limited by the state the brainstem is in.
Dr. Porges created a word for this: neuroception. It explains the phenomenon of hardwired autonomic shifts within the mammalian organism.

Hardwired is the key. There are predictable, even universal, ways that mammals react to various levels of safety and danger. That doesn't mean it looks the same for all of us. There's a wide variety in what it can look like. But as a living organism, you have hardwired responses based on what your senses are detecting. I don't like comparing us to computers, but it's the best analogy I have: press a certain button and you get a certain response. It's similar for us, not exactly the same, but similar. We're an organism primed to survive, always scanning for the potential to survive. Information comes in through the five senses, and primitive parts of the brain evaluate it for safety, danger, or life threat. These responses are unconscious and biologically hardwired. Again, not a choice.

Take the sound of somebody's voice. The sing-song quality of a voice is called vocal prosody. Right now, I can go up and I can go down. Me using a wider range of my voice is probably giving you a neuroception of safety. Even though you're just hearing my voice, you're neurocepting that Justin is a safe mammal, and that might help your autonomic nervous system get to the top of your polyvagal ladder and feel safer.

Monotone voices are different. They're typically a neuroception of danger. If I lost all my prosody and taught you the Polyvagal Theory in a flat, slow monotone, you might not feel very safe or very high on your ladder. (That was hard for me to do.) You might notice a shift as I speak in a monotone versus the more prosodic voice I usually use. You didn't choose to respond the way you responded. You just did. These responses are built within you.

Close your eyes if you like, and picture somebody with wide eyes. Their muscles are tense. Their head and neck are straight, and they're looking dead on at you. How do you feel about that? Does it bring you toward feeling more safe, or more defensive?
Now compare that to a baby who's cooing and smiling and giggling and looking you in the eyes. Does that bring you toward feelings of safety, or defense? It's a different experience, right?

Depending on what we neurocept as safe, dangerous, or life threatening, our own social or defensive behaviors are triggered as we drop down or climb up the ladder. When we're in a flight and fight state, we don't need social behavior, so that more or less gets turned off.

Neuroception is the body's ability to detect risk outside of our conscious awareness, and in my opinion it's pretty darn amazing. If we had to consciously decide safety or danger, we'd be too slow. Because it's autonomic, we can shift state quickly and respond, hopefully appropriately.

Neuroception shifts our state up and down the polyvagal ladder between those three primary states. As we move down the ladder, we lose access to the behaviors higher up. But moving down also unlocks defensive behaviors, which is actually really cool. It's kind of like a key. If we neurocept danger, we drop down the ladder, we lose access to our social behaviors, and it unlocks the capacity to run or fight.

If you're sitting there right now and a tiger walks in the room (I don't know why, it just does), I really hope you neurocept that as dangerous. Shifting down your ladder into flight energy increases your chances of surviving, because it unlocks a big old adrenaline rush to get the heck out of there. You don't need to pet the tiger. You don't need to smile at it and use your vocal prosody. You need to get out of that situation. It's adaptive. It's a good thing.
You might be thinking, "I don't respond to danger the way I'd like to," or "I don't detect safety the way I'd like to." The Polyvagal Theory breaks neuroception down into healthy and unhealthy.

With healthy neuroception, the body detects and shifts to the appropriate state based on the environment. In a safe environment, we neurocept safety, climb to the top of the ladder, and use pro-social behavior. We don't fight or run away in a safe environment. That's only for when we're actually in danger. With healthy neuroception, we're better at accurately identifying red flags and accurately identifying safety. We can feel safe with safe others, and we can mobilize when we need to. Say you go out on a date with your spouse. Ideally, you feel safe on the date and have access to your social behaviors. But if something happens, you're able to detect it, mobilize, and get to safety.

With unhealthy neuroception, the body doesn't accurately detect, and doesn't shift state based on the environment. It doesn't run or fight when it's in an unsafe situation, and it doesn't use safe and social behavior in a safe environment. There's a mismatch.

According to Dr. Porges, and I completely agree, unhealthy neuroception may be at the core of many mental health disorders. Not being able to detect safety, or access the safety pathways, would leave somebody in a defensive state: with flight and fight energy, or with the depletion, collapse and lack of energy of shutdown. That could look like many different mental health disorders. A lot of what's in the DSM might be better explained by where somebody is on their polyvagal ladder and whether their neuroception is more or less healthy.

With unhealthy neuroception, there are a lot of missed red flags. I work with a lot of teens, and their ability to recognize danger in a love interest is often very compromised. As they tell me about a boyfriend or girlfriend, red flags are going off for me left and right. They don't neurocept the danger in these people or in the environment they're in, until they're in their own safe and social state. After some therapy, when I explain, "This is what I'm hearing," they can say, "Oh yeah, now I see it." But only once they have access to their own safe and social state.

Another example comes up fairly often in my work with teens: a mom who was sexually abused then allows a short-term boyfriend to move in with her and her children. Her neuroception, her ability to detect safety or danger in her partner, is severely compromised. She's not picking up on how dangerous that could be.

Or you might be into yoga, and being still in yoga can actually feel like danger, even though it's literally safe. Someone with challenges neurocepting safety stays in a defensive state, even in a safe environment with safe people. Certain poses, or savasana at the end of class where you lie down and stay still, might keep them from climbing to the top of the ladder and feeling safe at the same time.

Or the kids in class who can't sit still, who are more concerned with who's saying what and who's looking at who. Classrooms aren't all safe, I know. But typically they're safe enough, with safe teachers and safe adults. The student's capacity to detect that is just compromised.
The final concept is story follows state, again from Deb Dana. Story follows state is the idea that our thoughts reflect the autonomic state we're in. Here's how she described it:

q: Polyvagal Theory in the clinical world is a paradigm shift. So we're asking people to look at things differently, and one of the things is that story follows state: that your autonomic state comes to life, and then the information's fed up to your brain, and your brain's job is to make sense of what's happening in the body. So it makes up a story. And the stories that emerge from dorsal, sympathetic and ventral are very different.
blocks.cite: Deb Dana, [Deb Dana Interview: Story Follows State, Climbing the Ladder and Diagnosing (episode 29)](https://player.captivate.fm/episode/f8b9643c-28f8-4185-9525-8b4e6301516c)

blocks.p: Our thoughts don't simply exist on their own. The story in our heads follows the state we're in.

ul: In the safe and social state, our thoughts are more hopeful. They involve more critical thinking, planning, and problem solving.

In flight and fight, our thoughts don't have much empathy. They're more fear-based, more about blaming or avoiding responsibility, more about who's out to get us. They won't be about slowing down and thinking critically. They're highly reactionary.

In shutdown, the thoughts are hopeless and very judgmental, especially toward the self. We still can't access critical thinking, weighing pros and cons, or seeing someone else's viewpoint. Those skills are lost, or at least compromised.

blocks.p: As Deb Dana says, "You can see how the story changes depending on my state, not depending on what I choose to think."

The story that follows the state might not reflect reality. Someone in a very shutdown state might have stories about how worthless they are. In my opinion, that's just not reality. When we're in fight energy and blaming someone for our problems, that might not be correct either. It could be. Not necessarily.

You've probably experienced this. You're really upset or really anxious one moment, and then later that day, or after you sleep and wake up the next day, you look back at the same situation and you feel differently about it. You think differently about it, because you're possibly not in that defensive state anymore. You have more access to your safe and social state, and when you reflect on the same situation, your thoughts are different. Your state has changed the story.

The story is an attempt to explain why our state is the way it is. "I'm pissed off because of that person." "I'm scared because of this situation." "I feel this way because I'm worthless." It reflects what's happening within us. It follows it.

blocks.h3: Two moments from my own life

blocks.p: A couple of years ago, I was in bed one night, not quite asleep. The lights were off in my room, and outside the room we had a hall light on for the kids. I saw a shadow creep toward my room. It was just the briefest of moments, but my body neurocepted danger. My muscles tensed, I held my breath, and my heartbeat picked up a little. I shifted, unconsciously, into a flight and fight kind of sympathetic energy. Then an image popped into my head: a burglar. Someone's robbing the house. Story follows state. My state changed first, without me being aware of it, and then the image of a burglar popped into my mind.
It ended up being my son. If you have kids, they often do very scary things at nighttime when you're trying to sleep.

Another time, I had a procedure done, which I won't go into, where I was numb but awake. During the procedure, I felt a shock, like a burn or some sort of electrical spark. The basic idea is that it was painful. Instantaneously, my heart rate kicked way up and my muscles flexed. I was lying on the procedure bed, and my body basically folded in half: torso up, legs up. I know it was a fight state, because I couldn't run away from this. I was in the middle of a procedure. I also know because of the story that popped into my mind, the words that came out of my mouth: "What the fuck?" Definitely fight energy. What are you doing? What is happening down there?

These are instantaneous, tiny moments where we neurocept safety, danger, or life threat. Our autonomic nervous system shifts, our body responds, it feels different, the experience is different, and our thoughts change as well. Those tiny moments can get stretched out, and we can get stuck in these feedback loops, these defense strategies. The bottom line is to think about feedback loops and ask the question: is the autonomic nervous system in a state of defense?

blocks.h: A new paradigm, and a new narrative

blocks.p: I know this is a lot of information. These are the foundations for going deeper into each of these states, into what trauma is, and into what the heck we do about all of this.
Here's what I want you to take away. The Polyvagal Theory is a new paradigm, and that's what I love about it. Dr. Porges described it with a metaphor:

q: There's almost a strange metaphor. It's like when they say batteries not included. In human beings, the manual wasn't included. And so it's really a retrospective development of a manual of what it is to be a human being. And Polyvagal Theory has some of these features.

blocks.p: It brings a new paradigm to mental health. To me, it fits alongside the DSM, but it's a different paradigm, and I think a more useful one. It's a way to look at us, and if you're a therapist, a way to look at your clients as being stuck in a defensive state rather than having some sort of disorder. Dr. Porges again:

q: I think what you would find is that it really doesn't matter what the diagnosis is, that they share some common features. And the common features have to do with state regulation. And in fact, the manifestation, whether it's DID or borderline, has to do with the strategy that the higher brain structures developed to regulate their state.

blocks.p: The Polyvagal Theory also brings a roadmap of change. Because we have the polyvagal ladder, we have some milestones for what change looks like. It's not a therapeutic modality in and of itself, but it's a way to track change and understand change. And it's a way to understand ourselves, as therapists, as parents, as teachers, in whatever role we have. It's a new way of looking at us and our interactions.

I really want to stress this: in my opinion, there's way more utility in the Polyvagal Theory than in other paradigms of mental health and relationships, with far less judgment. There's no judgment in this. It's just biology. That's it.
If we can learn this new paradigm and apply it to ourselves, it can create a new narrative. Dr. Porges explained why that matters:

q: So if we have these feelings, what do we make of those feelings? How do we use those feelings to create a reality? And the issue is the personal narrative. This is where Polyvagal Theory became useful to many people with a variety of disorders. It enabled them to inform their personal narrative that functionally there was a reason why they were experiencing these things. Then a different reality would start. In a sense, it was a self-healing process. If the higher brain structures, our cognitive sense of awareness, become attuned to what's going on in our body, and that makes sense in a psychoeducational way, then it creates a container on top of those feelings.

blocks.p: So the Polyvagal Theory can be a new narrative for you: for understanding yourself, how you feel, why you are the way you are and why you aren't the way you aren't. Without judgment. It is what it is for now, and it's an issue of being stuck, not broken.
